Start here: How to use this course

What this course is

This course teaches system design in a fixed order. Every lesson builds on the one before it. You do not need any background in distributed systems to start. By the end you will be able to take an open-ended question such as "Design Instagram" or "Design a rate limiter", ask the right questions, estimate the scale, draw the architecture, and explain the trade-offs under pressure.

The three levels

LevelWho it is forWhat you will be able to do
Beginner (Parts 1–2)You have built apps but never designed a large system.Explain requests, scaling, databases, caching, queues. Design a small system end to end.
Intermediate (Parts 3–4)You know the basics and want to handle failures and scale.Reason about replication, consensus, retries, idempotency, streams. Design feeds, payments, storage, and video.
Advanced (Part 5)You are preparing for senior or staff-level rounds.Choose architecture styles, plan operations, security, multi-region, cost.
Low-level design (Part 6)Coding-round candidates.Model classes, apply patterns, write working code with concurrency in mind.
Mastery (Part 7)Everyone, before the interview.Run the 45-minute interview clock, handle mistakes, tell your project stories, pass the final check.

How each lesson is laid out

  • Goal: what you will be able to do at the end.
  • The idea in plain words: an explanation with an everyday analogy.
  • Figure or code: a diagram, or a program you can run and its real output.
  • Step by step: the mechanism, slowly.
  • Check yourself: questions to answer without looking. Answers are at the end of each part.
Key idea. Do not move on until you can answer the Check-yourself questions out loud. If you cannot, reread the lesson once, then move on and come back to it in the final review.

The four boxes you will see

Plain words. A simple explanation or analogy. Read this first if a term is new.
Key idea. The one thing to remember from the lesson.
Common mistake. A trap that interviewers see often.
Interview tip. What to say, and how, when this topic comes up.

Suggested pace

Your situationPlan
Learning from scratchOne lesson a day for about 6 weeks, then Parts 6 and 7 for 2 weeks.
Some experienceParts 2–5 in 3 weeks, Part 6 in 1 week, Part 7 in 1 week.
Interview in 1 weekLesson 1, the framework in Lesson 38, the cheat sheets in the Appendix, and two mock interviews in Part 7.
Practice rule. Draw on paper. Say your answer out loud. Time yourself. Reading alone feels like learning but is not enough.

Level: Beginner · About 20 minutes

Lesson 1: What system design is

Goal

Understand what a system design interview tests, and the structure every answer should follow.

The idea in plain words

Plain words. Coding interviews ask "write a function that does X." System design interviews ask "build a service that serves millions of people." The question is vague on purpose. The interviewer wants to see how you turn a vague goal into a clear plan, and how you think about what can go wrong.

A system design answer is a conversation, not a speech. You ask questions, make assumptions explicit, draw a picture, go deeper where it matters, and talk about trade-offs.

What interviewers score

  • Requirements: did you clarify what to build before building it?
  • Estimation: do you know roughly how big the problem is?
  • Design: is the picture clear, with each part having a job?
  • Depth: can you explain how one hard part works?
  • Trade-offs: do you name what you gave up?
  • Communication: is your reasoning easy to follow?

Step by step: the six steps you will use every time

  1. Requirements (about 5 minutes): what must the system do, and what must it never do?
  2. Estimates (about 4 minutes): how many users, requests per second, data size?
  3. API and data (about 5 minutes): what calls does a user make, and what do we store?
  4. High-level design (about 11 minutes): boxes and arrows for the main flow.
  5. Deep dives (about 15 minutes): pick the hardest 2 or 3 parts and go deep.
  6. Wrap-up (about 3 minutes): what can fail, how we would monitor it, what we would build next.
Common mistake. Starting to draw boxes in the first minute. Without requirements you are designing for a system nobody asked for.
Interview tip. Open with: "Before I design, I'd like to clarify a few requirements. Then I'll estimate scale and sketch the main flow." Interviewers relax when you have a plan.

Check yourself

  1. Name the six steps in order.
  2. Why should you spend time on requirements before drawing anything?
  3. What does the interviewer usually want from the deep-dive section?
Level: Beginner · About 25 minutes

Lesson 2: How a request travels

Goal

Trace what happens from the moment a user taps a button to the moment they see a result.

The idea in plain words

Plain words. Think of ordering food. You look up the restaurant's address (DNS), you walk to the counter (load balancer), the cashier takes your order (the server), the kitchen checks if the dish is already prepared (the cache), and only if not, it cooks from the fridge (the database).

Step by step

  1. DNS: the phone turns a name like app.example.com into an IP address.
  2. Connection: the phone opens a secure connection (TCP and TLS). This takes a few round trips before any data moves.
  3. Load balancer: it picks one of many servers for this request.
  4. Application server: runs your business logic.
  5. Cache: a fast memory store is checked first.
  6. Database: only used when the cache does not have the answer.
  7. Response: the result travels back the same way.
Key idea. Each step adds time. A round trip across a continent is about 150 ms. A database query might be 5–20 ms. A memory lookup is about 0.0001 ms. Good design keeps the slow steps off the hot path.

Check yourself

  1. Why is the cache checked before the database?
  2. What does the load balancer do, in one sentence?
  3. Why does opening a connection cost time even when the server is fast?
Level: Beginner · About 25 minutes

Lesson 3: Scaling and load balancers

Goal

Know the two ways to scale, and why a load balancer is the first box you add when one server is not enough.

The idea in plain words

Plain words. A small shop with one cashier works until the queue is long. You can hire a faster cashier (vertical scaling), or open more tills and put a person at the door to send customers to the shortest queue (horizontal scaling plus a load balancer).

Vertical vs horizontal

Vertical (scale up)Horizontal (scale out)
What you doBuy a bigger machineAdd more machines
ProsSimple. No code changes.No hard ceiling. Survives one machine failing.
ConsA ceiling. One failure takes everything down.Needs routing, and shared state must be handled.

What a load balancer does

  1. Receives every incoming request.
  2. Picks a healthy server using an algorithm (for example, round robin, or least connections).
  3. Stops sending traffic to a server that fails its health check.
Key idea. Make your application servers stateless: they should not keep user session data in their own memory. Then any server can handle any request, and you can add or remove servers freely.
Common mistake. Saying "I'll scale horizontally" and stopping there. Always say what becomes shared (the database, the cache, sessions) and how you handle it.

Check yourself

  1. Name one advantage and one disadvantage of vertical scaling.
  2. Why should application servers be stateless?
  3. What happens to traffic when a load balancer's health check fails for one server?
Level: Beginner · About 30 minutes

Lesson 4: Numbers you must know

Goal

Estimate traffic, storage, and bandwidth in two minutes, and know how fast each kind of operation is.

The idea in plain words

Plain words. You do not need exact numbers. You need the right order of magnitude. Is it 10 requests per second or 10,000? That difference decides the whole design.

The numbers

ThingValue to remember
Seconds per dayAbout 86,400. Use 105 for quick math.
Memory accessAbout 100 nanoseconds
SSD random readAbout 100 microseconds
Round trip inside a data centerAbout 0.5 ms
Round trip across continentsAbout 150 ms

Estimation, step by step

Example: a social app with 10 million daily users, each opening the app 5 times a day, each open making 10 requests.

  1. Daily requests: 10M × 5 × 10 = 500 million.
  2. Average per second: 500M ÷ 105 ≈ 5,000 requests per second.
  3. Peak: assume 3× average, so about 15,000 per second.
  4. Say it out loud: "About 5,000 average, about 15,000 at peak. That tells me I need several servers and a cache."
Key idea. Always compute an average, then a peak (usually 2 to 3 times the average), and say what each number means for the design.
Common mistake. Giving a precise-looking number such as "4,167 requests per second" with no reason. Round it. Interviewers want the reasoning, not false precision.

Check yourself

  1. How many seconds are in a day, roughly?
  2. Estimate the average requests per second for 2 million daily users making 20 requests each.
  3. Why is a cross-continent call a problem on a hot path?
Level: Beginner · About 30 minutes

Lesson 5: Databases and indexes

Goal

Choose between SQL and NoSQL at a basic level, and understand why an index makes reads faster but writes slower.

The idea in plain words

Plain words. A database is a filing cabinet. An index is the card catalogue at the front of a library. Without it, finding a book means checking every shelf. With it, you go straight to the right shelf, but each new book needs a catalogue card too.

SQL vs NoSQL

SQL (PostgreSQL, MySQL)NoSQL (Cassandra, DynamoDB, MongoDB)
Shape of dataTables with fixed columnsFlexible: key-value, documents, wide columns
StrengthJoins, transactions, constraintsVery high scale, simple access by key
Choose whenRelationships and correctness matter (orders, money, users)Massive writes, known access pattern (events, sessions, timelines)

How an index works

  1. An index is a sorted copy of one or more columns.
  2. Each entry points to the full row.
  3. A search on the indexed column becomes a fast lookup instead of a full scan.
  4. Every insert or update must also update the index, so writes cost more.
Key idea. A composite index on (city, age) helps "city = Pune" and "city = Pune and age = 30". It does not help "age = 30" alone, because the data is sorted by city first. Like a phone book sorted by surname, then first name.
Common mistake. Adding an index to every column. Each index slows writes and takes storage. Index the columns your queries actually filter on.

Check yourself

  1. Give one reason to choose SQL for a bank ledger.
  2. Why does an index slow down writes?
  3. Would an index on (city, age) help a query that filters only by age? Why?
Level: Beginner · About 30 minutes

Lesson 6: Caching

Goal

Use the cache-aside pattern correctly, and calculate how much a cache improves average latency.

The idea in plain words

Plain words. A cache is the notes you keep on your desk. Looking something up in your own notes is faster than walking to the archive. The risk: the notes can go out of date.

The cache-aside pattern

  1. Read: check the cache. If found (a hit), return it.
  2. Read miss: read the database, put the value in the cache, return it.
  3. Write: update the database first, then delete the cache entry.

Why delete instead of update on write

Two requests can race. If you update the cache, an old value can end up in it and stay there. If you delete it, the next read fetches the fresh value from the database.

Hit ratio math

Average latency = hit ratio × cache time + (1 − hit ratio) × database time.

With a 95% hit ratio: 0.95 × 1 + 0.05 × 20 = 1.95 ms. With 80%: 0.8 × 1 + 0.2 × 20 = 4.8 ms. The database is only 20× slower, yet the average more than doubles.

Key idea. The hit ratio is the most important number for a cache. Protect it.
Common mistake. Caching everything with no expiry. Stale data will hurt users. Set a time-to-live (TTL) and say how stale the data may be.

Check yourself

  1. Walk through cache-aside on a read miss.
  2. Why delete the cache key on write instead of updating it?
  3. Compute the average latency for a 90% hit ratio, a 2 ms cache, and a 30 ms database.
Level: Beginner · About 45 minutes · Practice lesson

Lesson 7: Your first design: a URL shortener

Goal

Run the full six-step framework on a real question, from start to finish.

The question

"Design a URL shortener like bit.ly. A user gives a long link and gets a short one. Visiting the short link redirects to the long one."

Step 1: Requirements

  • Create a short link from a long URL.
  • Redirect a short link to the original URL.
  • Optional: custom alias, expiry date, click count.
  • Redirects must be fast (under 50 ms at p99). Redirects are much more common than creates.
  • Out of scope for now: user accounts, malware scanning.

Step 2: Estimates

  • 100 million new links per month: about 100M ÷ 2.6M seconds ≈ 40 writes per second, peak about 120.
  • Read to write ratio 100 to 1: about 4,000 reads per second on average, peak about 12,000.
  • Storage: 500 bytes per link × 100M per month ≈ 600 GB per year.

Step 3: API and data

  • POST /urls with a long URL, returns a short code.
  • GET /{code} returns a redirect.
  • Data: a key-value table keyed by the short code, with the long URL and an expiry.

Step 4: Making the short code

Use a counter, not a hash of the URL. A hash can collide, and the same URL would always produce the same code, which leaks information. A unique number encoded in base 62 (letters, digits) gives 627 ≈ 3.5 trillion codes with only seven characters. Servers take blocks of 10,000 numbers from a counter service, so they do not ask for a number on every request.

One way to get unique numbers without asking a central counter for each one is a Snowflake-style ID: a timestamp, a machine number, and a sequence number packed into one 64-bit value. Here is a small version:

Code (runs with Python 3, standard library only)
import threading as _th

class Snowflake:
    EPOCH = 1700000000000  # ms
    def __init__(self, machine_id: int):
        self.machine = machine_id & 0x3FF   # 10 bits
        self.seq = 0
        self.last = -1
        self.lock = _th.Lock()

    def next_id(self, now_ms: int) -> int:
        with self.lock:
            if now_ms == self.last:
                self.seq = (self.seq + 1) & 0xFFF   # 12 bits
                if self.seq == 0:
                    raise RuntimeError("sequence exhausted this ms; wait")
            else:
                self.seq = 0
            self.last = now_ms
            return ((now_ms - self.EPOCH) << 22) | (self.machine << 12) | self.seq

gen = Snowflake(machine_id=7)
ids = [gen.next_id(1700000001000) for _ in range(3)] + [gen.next_id(1700000001001)]
print("ids:", ids)
print("strictly increasing:", all(a < b for a, b in zip(ids, ids[1:])))
Output when you run it:
ids: [4194332672, 4194332673, 4194332674, 4198526976]
strictly increasing: True

Step 5: High-level design

Step 6: Deep dives and wrap-up

  • Hot link: one link gets 50,000 requests per second. Add a small in-memory cache on each redirect server.
  • Expiry: check the expiry on read. Clean up expired links in batches later, not by scanning the whole table.
  • Failure: if the cache is down, reads fall through to the database and become slower but still work.
  • Analytics: send click events to a queue and count them later. Redirects never wait for counting.
Key idea. Separate the read path from the write path. Reads are 100 times more common, so they get the cache and the most servers.

Check yourself

  1. Why use a counter instead of hashing the long URL?
  2. Why is the redirect service separate from the create service?
  3. What happens to redirects if the cache fails?

Level: Beginner to intermediate · About 30 minutes

Lesson 8: Replication and failover

Goal

Explain why data is copied to several machines, how a failover works, and what can be lost in the process.

The idea in plain words

Plain words. Keep copies of an important document in several safe places. If one burns down, another copy is still there. The catch: if you copy the document after every edit, you wait for the copies to finish. If you do not wait, a crash can lose the last edit.

Leader and followers

  • One node is the leader. It accepts all writes.
  • The other nodes are followers. They copy the leader's change log and serve reads.
  • If the leader dies, a follower is promoted to leader. This is a failover.

Synchronous vs asynchronous

SynchronousAsynchronous
How the leader repliesWaits for a follower to confirmReplies right away
SpeedSlowerFaster
Risk on failoverNo acknowledged write is lostThe last few acknowledged writes can be lost
Key idea. Asynchronous replication is fast but can lose the most recent writes during failover. Say which one you chose and why. For payments you usually choose synchronous or a quorum; for a like counter, asynchronous is fine.

Step by step: a failover

  1. Followers notice the leader has stopped sending heartbeats for longer than a timeout.
  2. The most up-to-date follower is chosen as the new leader.
  3. Clients are pointed at the new leader.
  4. The old leader must be fenced off. If it comes back, it must not accept writes (Lesson 14 explains how).
Common mistake. Saying "we replicate, so we never lose data". Ask: synchronous or asynchronous? What is the window of possible loss?

Check yourself

  1. What is a failover?
  2. Why can asynchronous replication lose an acknowledged write?
  3. Which replication style would you choose for a bank balance, and why?
Level: Beginner to intermediate · About 40 minutes

Lesson 9: Sharding and consistent hashing

Goal

Split data across machines, choose a shard key, and explain why consistent hashing moves few keys when servers change.

The idea in plain words

Plain words. A library too big for one building is split into branches. You need a rule to know which branch holds which book. Sharding is that split. Consistent hashing is a rule that rarely needs to be rewritten when a branch opens or closes.

Sharding basics

  • Range sharding: users A–H on shard 1, I–Q on shard 2. Simple, but timestamps all land on the newest shard (a hot spot).
  • Hash sharding: shard = hash(key) mod N. Even spread, but adding a shard moves almost every key.
  • Consistent hashing: servers and keys sit on a ring. Adding a server moves only a small share of keys.

Why virtual nodes

With only a few servers, one server can end up with a large arc. Each server is placed at many points (for example 100 or 200 virtual nodes) so the load evens out.

Code (runs with Python 3, standard library only)
import bisect, hashlib, collections

def h(s: str) -> int:
    return int(hashlib.md5(s.encode()).hexdigest(), 16)

class Ring:
    def __init__(self, vnodes=100):
        self.vnodes = vnodes
        self.keys = []      # sorted hash positions on the ring
        self.owner = {}     # position -> physical node name

    def add(self, node):
        for i in range(self.vnodes):
            p = h(f"{node}#{i}")
            bisect.insort(self.keys, p)
            self.owner[p] = node

    def remove(self, node):
        for i in range(self.vnodes):
            p = h(f"{node}#{i}")
            self.keys.remove(p)
            del self.owner[p]

    def lookup(self, key: str) -> str:
        p = h(key)
        i = bisect.bisect_right(self.keys, p) % len(self.keys)  # next clockwise
        return self.owner[self.keys[i]]

ring = Ring(vnodes=100)
for n in ["A", "B", "C", "D"]:
    ring.add(n)
keys = [f"user:{i}" for i in range(10000)]
before = {k: ring.lookup(k) for k in keys}
print("load per node:", dict(collections.Counter(before.values())))
ring.add("E")
after = {k: ring.lookup(k) for k in keys}
moved = sum(before[k] != after[k] for k in keys)
print(f"after adding E: {moved/len(keys):.1%} of keys moved (ideal ~20%)")
print("all moved keys now live on E:", all(after[k]=="E" for k in keys if before[k]!=after[k]))
Output when you run it:
load per node: {'B': 2466, 'A': 2577, 'C': 2509, 'D': 2448}
after adding E: 18.9% of keys moved (ideal ~20%)
all moved keys now live on E: True
Key idea. In the output, adding server E moved about one fifth of the keys (about 1 in 5 with five servers), and every moved key went to E. Nothing else reshuffled.
Common mistake. Choosing a shard key with uneven traffic, such as a celebrity user ID or a single big tenant. One shard then does most of the work. Pick a key with many distinct values and an even access pattern.

Check yourself

  1. Why is a timestamp a poor shard key for write-heavy data?
  2. What moves when you add one server to a hash ring?
  3. Why use virtual nodes?
Level: Beginner to intermediate · About 35 minutes

Lesson 10: Consistency in plain words

Goal

Understand quorums, the CAP choice, and the consistency levels you can promise a user.

The idea in plain words

Plain words. Two bank branches share a ledger. If the phone line between them breaks, one branch must choose: stop serving customers until the line is fixed (consistent but unavailable), or keep serving with a slightly outdated ledger (available but possibly wrong). That choice is CAP.

Quorums: reading the latest write

Store three copies. A write is confirmed when two copies accept it (W = 2). A read asks two copies (R = 2). Because 2 + 2 is greater than 3, the two copies you read must include at least one copy that has the newest write.

Key idea. R + W greater than N means reads see the latest confirmed write. Write it on the board: N = 3, W = 2, R = 2 works.
Code (runs with Python 3, standard library only)
def quorum_ok(n, w, r):
    return r + w > n

for n, w, r in [(3,2,2), (3,1,1), (5,3,3), (5,2,2)]:
    print(f"N={n} W={w} R={r}: R+W>N is {quorum_ok(n,w,r)}  -> reads see latest write: {quorum_ok(n,w,r)}")
Output when you run it:
N=3 W=2 R=2: R+W>N is True  -> reads see latest write: True
N=3 W=1 R=1: R+W>N is False  -> reads see latest write: False
N=5 W=3 R=3: R+W>N is True  -> reads see latest write: True
N=5 W=2 R=2: R+W>N is False  -> reads see latest write: False

CAP in one sentence

When the network splits, you choose between refusing some requests (consistency) or answering with possibly old data (availability). Without a split, the real trade-off is latency against consistency (PACELC).

Consistency levels to name in interviews

  • Strong: every read sees the latest write. Needed for balances, inventory, unique usernames.
  • Read-your-writes: after you post a comment, you see it. Achieve by reading from the leader for a short time after a write.
  • Eventual: everyone converges later. Fine for like counts and view counts.
Common mistake. "Pick two of CAP forever." CAP only applies during a partition, and most of the time you can have both.

Check yourself

  1. With N = 5 copies, give a W and R that guarantee reads see the latest write.
  2. Pick a consistency level for a like counter, and one for a bank balance.
  3. What does CAP ask you to choose, and when?
Level: Beginner to intermediate · About 35 minutes

Lesson 11: Transactions and isolation

Goal

Recognize the two classic concurrency bugs (lost update and write skew) and know how to prevent each.

The idea in plain words

Plain words. Two people edit the same shared spreadsheet at the same moment. Without a rule, one person's changes can silently overwrite the other's. A transaction groups changes so they all happen or none do, and isolation decides what each person can see of the other's unfinished work.

Bug 1: lost update

  1. Balance is 100. Alice reads 100. Bob reads 100.
  2. Alice writes 100 − 30 = 70.
  3. Bob writes 100 − 50 = 50. Alice's withdrawal has vanished.

Fix: lock the row while you read and write (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE), or use a version number and retry if it changed.

Bug 2: write skew

Rule: at least one doctor must stay on call. Doctor A and Doctor B are both on call. Both check "is someone else on call?" (yes), and both go off call. Nobody is on call. Each transaction looked fine on its own snapshot.

Fix: serializable isolation, or lock the shared rows that the rule depends on.

Isolation levels in one table

LevelWhat it preventsStill allows
Read committedReading unfinished dataLost updates, write skew
SnapshotMost read anomaliesWrite skew
SerializableEverythingNothing, but slower
Key idea. Name the anomaly before you name the fix. "This is a lost update, so I'll use a conditional update with a version" is a strong answer.

Check yourself

  1. Describe a lost update in three steps.
  2. Why does snapshot isolation allow write skew?
  3. Give a fix for a lost update that does not lock anything.
Level: Beginner to intermediate · About 30 minutes

Lesson 12: Queues and asynchronous work

Goal

Use a queue to take slow work off the request path, and understand the difference between a queue and a log.

The idea in plain words

Plain words. A restaurant takes your order and gives you a ticket. The kitchen works through tickets at its own pace. You do not wait at the counter while your dish is cooked. A queue is the rail where tickets wait.

Why queues help

  • Speed: the user gets a fast reply ("order received") while slow work happens later (sending emails, resizing images).
  • Smoothing: a burst of 10,000 requests becomes a steady stream the workers can handle.
  • Safety: if a worker crashes, the message is still in the queue and can be retried.

Queue or log?

Queue (SQS, RabbitMQ)Log (Kafka)
After a worker reads a messageIt is removedIt stays, and other readers can read it too
Replay old messagesUsually noYes
Best forTasks done once (send email)Events many teams use (analytics, feeds)
Common mistake. Forgetting that a retried message can arrive twice. Workers must be safe to run twice (Lesson 16 covers this).

Check yourself

  1. Name a task that should run in a queue, and say why.
  2. What does a queue absorb during a traffic spike?
  3. Why is a log better than a queue for analytics that several teams use?
Level: Intermediate · About 50 minutes · Practice lesson

Lesson 13: Your second design: a rate limiter

Goal

Design a rate limiter that protects an API, and implement the two most common algorithms.

The question

"Design a rate limiter that allows each API key a fixed number of requests and returns 429 when the limit is exceeded. It must work across many servers."

Step 1: Clarify

  • Limit per API key (and per IP for anonymous traffic).
  • Allow short bursts, but keep the long-run average under the limit.
  • Latency overhead under 1 ms. Accuracy within a few percent.
  • If the limiter store is down: choose fail-open for public read APIs, fail-closed for costly writes. Say which, and why.

Step 2: Algorithm, step by step

Token bucket

Plain words. A bucket holds tokens up to a capacity. Tokens drip in at a steady rate. Each request takes one token. If the bucket is empty, the request is rejected.
Code (runs with Python 3, standard library only)
import time

class TokenBucket:
    def __init__(self, capacity: float, refill_per_sec: float, now=time.monotonic):
        self.capacity, self.rate, self.now = capacity, refill_per_sec, now
        self.tokens, self.last = capacity, now()

    def allow(self, cost: float = 1.0) -> bool:
        t = self.now()
        self.tokens = min(self.capacity, self.tokens + (t - self.last) * self.rate)
        self.last = t
        if self.tokens >= cost:
            self.tokens -= cost
            return True
        return False

# Deterministic demo with a fake clock
clock = [0.0]
tb = TokenBucket(capacity=5, refill_per_sec=1, now=lambda: clock[0])
print("burst of 7 at t=0:", [tb.allow() for _ in range(7)])
clock[0] = 2.0
print("after 2 seconds, 2 more:", [tb.allow() for _ in range(3)])
Output when you run it:
burst of 7 at t=0: [True, True, True, True, True, False, False]
after 2 seconds, 2 more: [True, True, False]

Sliding window counter

With a limit of 100 per minute, a fixed window lets 200 requests through in two seconds when a burst straddles the minute boundary. A sliding window counter weights the previous window to fix this cheaply.

Code (runs with Python 3, standard library only)
class SlidingWindowCounter:
    """Approximates a sliding window using two fixed windows."""
    def __init__(self, limit: int, window: float, now):
        self.limit, self.window, self.now = limit, window, now
        self.curr_idx, self.curr, self.prev = -1, 0, 0

    def allow(self) -> bool:
        t = self.now()
        idx = int(t // self.window)
        if idx != self.curr_idx:
            self.prev = self.curr if idx == self.curr_idx + 1 else 0
            self.curr, self.curr_idx = 0, idx
        elapsed = (t % self.window) / self.window
        estimate = self.prev * (1 - elapsed) + self.curr
        if estimate < self.limit:
            self.curr += 1
            return True
        return False

clock = [0.0]
sw = SlidingWindowCounter(limit=10, window=60, now=lambda: clock[0])
clock[0] = 59.0
print("first 10 in window 0 ->", sum(sw.allow() for _ in range(10)))
clock[0] = 61.0
print("at t=61 (just after boundary), allowed:", sum(sw.allow() for _ in range(10)), "of 10 (previous window still weighs in)")
Output when you run it:
first 10 in window 0 -> 10
at t=61 (just after boundary), allowed: 1 of 10 (previous window still weighs in)

Step 3: Where it runs and how it scales

  • Run the check in the API gateway, so every service is protected in one place.
  • Store counters in a shared fast store (Redis). Use an atomic script so two servers cannot both take the last token.
  • Read the server's clock inside the script, so skewed clocks on app servers cannot grant extra tokens.
Key idea. The check must be atomic. Read-check-write done in three separate calls lets two requests both pass.
Common mistake. Counting in the application database. It is slow under load, and hot keys cause locking.

Check yourself

  1. What does the token bucket allow that a fixed window does not?
  2. Why must the check-and-decrement be atomic?
  3. Would you fail open or closed for a payment API? Why?

Machines fail, messages repeat, and clocks disagree. These lessons show how good designs cope.

Lesson 14: Leaders, consensus, and fencing

Goal

Explain how a group of machines agrees on one leader, and why a paused leader must be stopped from writing.

The idea in plain words

Plain words. A committee elects a chair. A candidate needs more than half the votes, so two chairs can never both be legitimate. Each term of office has a number, and anyone holding an old term is ignored.

Raft, step by step

  1. Every node is a follower and waits for a heartbeat from the leader.
  2. If the heartbeat stops, a node waits a random time, then becomes a candidate for a new term and asks for votes.
  3. A node that receives a majority of votes becomes leader.
  4. The leader sends log entries to followers. An entry is committed when a majority has stored it.
Key idea. A group of 5 tolerates 2 failures, because the remaining 3 are still a majority. A group of 7 tolerates 3.

The paused leader problem

A leader can pause (garbage collection, a slow network) and wake up believing it is still leader. A lock or lease expires in the meantime, so a second client takes over. Now two clients can write.

Code (runs with Python 3, standard library only)
class Storage:
    def __init__(self):
        self.highest = 0
        self.data = None
    def write(self, token, value):
        if token < self.highest:
            return f"REJECTED (token {token} < seen {self.highest})"
        self.highest = token
        self.data = value
        return "OK"

class LockService:
    def __init__(self): self.token = 0
    def acquire(self):
        self.token += 1
        return self.token

lock = LockService(); store = Storage()
t1 = lock.acquire()          # client 1 gets token 1, then pauses (GC)
t2 = lock.acquire()          # lease expired, client 2 gets token 2
print("client 2 writes:", store.write(t2, "from client 2"))
print("client 1 wakes and writes:", store.write(t1, "from client 1 (stale!)"))
print("stored value:", store.data)
Output when you run it:
client 2 writes: OK
client 1 wakes and writes: REJECTED (token 1 < seen 2)
stored value: from client 2
Common mistake. Using a lock with an expiry and assuming the lock is safe. Without a fencing token, a paused holder can still write. Lock services help, but the protected resource must check tokens.

Check yourself

  1. How many failures does a 7-node group tolerate?
  2. When is a Raft log entry committed?
  3. Why does a fencing token stop a paused client, even though its lease expired?
Level: Intermediate · About 40 minutes

Lesson 15: Timeouts, retries, and circuit breakers

Goal

Protect your system when a dependency is slow or failing: set timeouts, retry safely, and stop calling a broken service.

The idea in plain words

Plain words. If a shop's card machine is down, you do not keep swiping every second. You wait a bit, try again a few times, and if it still fails, you stop trying for a while and pay another way. Those three ideas are timeouts, backoff, and a circuit breaker.

Timeouts

Every call to another service needs a deadline. Without one, a slow dependency holds your threads until your whole service is stuck. Derive the timeout from the dependency's normal p99 latency plus a margin.

Retries with backoff and jitter

Retrying immediately makes an overloaded service worse. Wait a random time between zero and a cap that doubles each attempt. The randomness (jitter) spreads retries out.

Code (runs with Python 3, standard library only)
import random

def retry(fn, attempts=5, base=0.1, cap=2.0, sleep=time.sleep):
    for attempt in range(attempts):
        try:
            return fn()
        except IOError:
            if attempt == attempts - 1:
                raise
            # "full jitter": random wait between 0 and the exponential cap
            sleep(random.uniform(0, min(cap, base * 2 ** attempt)))

random.seed(1)
calls = []
def flaky_then_ok():
    calls.append(1)
    if len(calls) < 3:
        raise IOError("503")
    return "ok"
print("result:", retry(flaky_then_ok, sleep=lambda s: print(f"  waited {s:.3f}s")), "after", len(calls), "calls")
Output when you run it:
  waited 0.013s
  waited 0.169s
result: ok after 3 calls
Common mistake. Retrying at every layer. Three layers with three retries each send 27 times the load to the bottom service. Retry in one place, usually close to the caller.

Circuit breaker

After repeated failures, the breaker opens and calls fail instantly. After a cool-down, a trial call decides whether to close it again.

Code (runs with Python 3, standard library only)
class CircuitBreaker:
    def __init__(self, failure_threshold=3, cooldown=5.0, now=time.monotonic):
        self.th, self.cooldown, self.now = failure_threshold, cooldown, now
        self.state, self.failures, self.opened_at = "CLOSED", 0, 0.0

    def call(self, fn):
        if self.state == "OPEN":
            if self.now() - self.opened_at >= self.cooldown:
                self.state = "HALF_OPEN"
            else:
                raise RuntimeError("circuit open: failing fast")
        try:
            result = fn()
        except Exception:
            self.failures += 1
            if self.state == "HALF_OPEN" or self.failures >= self.th:
                self.state, self.opened_at = "OPEN", self.now()
            raise
        self.state, self.failures = "CLOSED", 0
        return result

clock = [0.0]
cb = CircuitBreaker(failure_threshold=3, cooldown=5, now=lambda: clock[0])
def flaky(): raise IOError("timeout")
for i in range(4):
    try: cb.call(flaky)
    except Exception as e: print(f"call {i+1}: {type(e).__name__}: {e}  state={cb.state}")
clock[0] = 6.0
try:
    cb.call(lambda: "ok")
    print("after cool-down, trial succeeded, state =", cb.state)
except Exception as e:
    print("unexpected", e)
Output when you run it:
call 1: OSError: timeout  state=CLOSED
call 2: OSError: timeout  state=CLOSED
call 3: OSError: timeout  state=OPEN
call 4: RuntimeError: circuit open: failing fast  state=OPEN
after cool-down, trial succeeded, state = CLOSED
Key idea. Only retry operations that are safe to repeat (see Lesson 16). A retry of a non-idempotent call can charge a customer twice.

Check yourself

  1. Why is an immediate retry dangerous during an outage?
  2. What does the circuit breaker do in the open state?
  3. Why do you need both a timeout and a retry limit?
Level: Intermediate · About 50 minutes

Lesson 16: Idempotency, outbox, and sagas

Goal

Make an operation safe to repeat, publish events without losing or inventing them, and undo a multi-step business action when a step fails.

Idempotency

Plain words. Pressing the lift button twice does not call two lifts. An idempotent operation gives the same result no matter how many times you ask. Networks repeat requests, so your payment API must behave like the lift button.

Pattern: the client sends an idempotency key (a unique ID for this attempt). The server stores the key with its result. A repeat with the same key returns the saved result. The same key with a different body is rejected.

Code (runs with Python 3, standard library only)
import threading

class IdempotentPayments:
    def __init__(self):
        self._lock = threading.Lock()
        self._results = {}   # idempotency_key -> (request_hash, response)
        self.charges = 0

    def pay(self, key: str, amount_minor: int) -> dict:
        req_hash = str(amount_minor)
        with self._lock:                      # check and store are atomic
            if key in self._results:
                saved_hash, saved = self._results[key]
                if saved_hash != req_hash:
                    return {"error": "422: key reused with different body"}
                return {**saved, "replayed": True}
            self.charges += 1                 # the one real side effect
            resp = {"status": "CAPTURED", "amount": amount_minor, "charge_no": self.charges}
            self._results[key] = (req_hash, resp)
            return {**resp, "replayed": False}

p = IdempotentPayments()
print(p.pay("order-42", 50000))
print(p.pay("order-42", 50000))   # network retry with same key
print(p.pay("order-42", 99999))   # same key, different body
print("real charges made:", p.charges)
Output when you run it:
{'status': 'CAPTURED', 'amount': 50000, 'charge_no': 1, 'replayed': False}
{'status': 'CAPTURED', 'amount': 50000, 'charge_no': 1, 'replayed': True}
{'error': '422: key reused with different body'}
real charges made: 1

Transactional outbox

Problem: you save an order to the database, then publish an event to Kafka. If the process crashes between the two, the order exists but no event was sent (or the reverse).

Code (runs with Python 3, standard library only)
import sqlite3, json

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, status TEXT)")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE outbox (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT, payload TEXT, sent INTEGER DEFAULT 0)")

def place_order(order_id, fail_after_insert=False):
    with db:  # one transaction: both writes or neither
        db.execute("INSERT INTO orders VALUES (?, 'PLACED')", (order_id,))
        db.execute("INSERT INTO outbox (payload) VALUES (?)", (json.dumps({"event": "OrderPlaced", "id": order_id}),))
        if fail_after_insert:
            raise RuntimeError("crash before commit")

def relay(publish):
    rows = db.execute("SELECT id, payload FROM outbox WHERE sent=0 ORDER BY id").fetchall()
    for rid, payload in rows:
        publish(payload)                      # at-least-once: may resend after a crash
        db.execute("UPDATE outbox SET sent=1 WHERE id=?", (rid,))
    db.commit()

try:
    place_order(1, fail_after_insert=True)
except RuntimeError:
    pass
print("after crash: orders =", db.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders").fetchone()[0],
      "| outbox =", db.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM outbox").fetchone()[0], "(nothing half-written)")
place_order(2)
sent = []
relay(sent.append)
print("published events:", sent)
Output when you run it:
after crash: orders = 0 | outbox = 0 (nothing half-written)
published events: ['{"event": "OrderPlaced", "id": 2}']

Saga

Booking a seat, charging a card, and sending a ticket cannot share one database transaction across services. A saga runs each step and, if a later step fails, runs the undo steps in reverse order.

Code (runs with Python 3, standard library only)
class SagaFailed(Exception): pass

def run_saga(steps):
    """steps: list of (name, action, compensation). Compensate completed steps in reverse."""
    done = []
    try:
        for name, action, comp in steps:
            action()
            done.append((name, comp))
            print(f"  ok: {name}")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"  FAILED: {e}; compensating")
        for name, comp in reversed(done):
            comp()
            print(f"  undone: {name}")
        raise SagaFailed(str(e))

def fail(): raise RuntimeError("email service down")
try:
    run_saga([
        ("reserve seat", lambda: None, lambda: None),
        ("charge card",  lambda: None, lambda: print("    refund issued")),
        ("send ticket",  fail,          lambda: None),
    ])
except SagaFailed:
    print("saga ended in a consistent state (seat released, card refunded)")
Output when you run it:
  ok: reserve seat
  ok: charge card
  FAILED: email service down; compensating
    refund issued
  undone: charge card
  undone: reserve seat
saga ended in a consistent state (seat released, card refunded)
Key idea. The three tools go together: idempotency makes retries safe, the outbox makes events reliable, and sagas make multi-step work recoverable.
Common mistake. Saying "exactly once" delivery. Networks can always repeat a message. Aim for "exactly-once effect": at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing.

Check yourself

  1. Why is pressing a payment button twice dangerous without an idempotency key?
  2. What problem does the outbox solve?
  3. In a saga, what happens when the last step fails?
Level: Intermediate · About 45 minutes

Lesson 17: Kafka and event streams

Goal

Explain topics, partitions, consumer groups, offsets, and the delivery guarantees you can configure.

The idea in plain words

Plain words. A Kafka topic is a set of numbered logbooks. Each logbook (partition) is written in order and never edited. Readers keep a bookmark (offset). A team of readers (consumer group) splits the logbooks between them, one reader per logbook.

The rules to know

  • Order holds only inside one partition. Use a key (for example the order ID) so all events for one order go to the same partition.
  • Parallelism is limited by partitions. Five partitions support at most five active consumers in a group.
  • Acknowledgements: acks=all with min in-sync replicas of 2 and replication factor 3 survives one broker failure without losing acknowledged messages.
  • Duplicates: a consumer that crashes after processing but before committing its offset will process the message again. Make consumers idempotent.
  • Retention: messages stay for a set time, so you can replay them.
Key idea. Choose the partition key to match the ordering you need. Changing the number of partitions later changes which partition each key goes to.
Common mistake. Using a random key. Events for the same entity then land on different partitions and can be processed out of order.

Check yourself

  1. Why would a consumer process a message twice?
  2. You have 12 partitions and 20 consumers in one group. How many consumers are busy?
  3. Which key would you use for a bank transaction stream, and why?
Level: Intermediate · About 45 minutes

Lesson 18: Stream processing, time, and late data

Goal

Count events by the time they happened, close windows correctly, and handle events that arrive late.

The idea in plain words

Plain words. A friend posts a photo of a sunset at 6:00 pm, but their phone was offline and it reaches you at 6:20 pm. If you count it under "posts at 6:20", your chart is wrong. Count it under the time it happened. The question is how long you wait for stragglers before you publish a number.

Key terms

  • Event time: when it happened. Processing time: when your system saw it. Use event time for correct charts.
  • Window: a bucket of time, such as one minute.
  • Watermark: the system's belief about how far behind the events are. When the watermark passes the end of a window (plus an allowed lateness), the window closes.
  • Late event: an event that arrives after its window closed. Send it to a correction path rather than silently changing a published number.
Code (runs with Python 3, standard library only)
from collections import defaultdict

class MinuteCounter:
    """Counts events per minute (by EVENT time). Closes a window when watermark passes it."""
    def __init__(self, allowed_lateness=300):
        self.windows = defaultdict(int)
        self.closed = set()
        self.watermark = 0
        self.lateness = allowed_lateness
        self.corrections = []

    def on_event(self, event_time: int):
        minute = event_time // 60 * 60
        if minute in self.closed:
            self.corrections.append(event_time)     # too late: do not change published number
            return
        self.windows[minute] += 1
        self.watermark = max(self.watermark, event_time)
        for m in list(self.windows):
            if m + 60 + self.lateness <= self.watermark:
                self.closed.add(m)
                print(f"  window {m} closed with count {self.windows[m]}")

mc = MinuteCounter(allowed_lateness=300)
for t in [30, 45, 70, 80, 100]:
    mc.on_event(t)
mc.on_event(900)                  # watermark jumps to 15:00
mc.on_event(40)                   # very late event for minute 0
print("late events sent to correction path:", mc.corrections)
Output when you run it:
  window 0 closed with count 2
  window 60 closed with count 3
late events sent to correction path: [40]
Key idea. Allowed lateness is a trade-off: longer means more accurate numbers but slower results. Choose it per use case and say so.

Check yourself

  1. Why is event time better than processing time for a per-minute chart?
  2. What closes a window?
  3. What should happen to a very late event, and why?
Level: Intermediate · About 60 minutes · Practice lesson

Lesson 19: Your third design: a chat application

Goal

Design a messaging system with online delivery, ordering, read receipts, and offline push, using the ideas from Parts 2 and 3.

The question

"Design a chat app like WhatsApp: one-to-one and group messages, delivery and read receipts, online status, message history."

Step 1: Requirements

  • Messages arrive in order within a conversation.
  • Online delivery under about 300 ms within a region.
  • Offline users get a push notification and catch up when they reconnect.
  • History is kept forever.

Step 2: Estimates

  • 50 million daily users × 40 messages ≈ 2 billion messages a day, about 23,000 per second on average, about 70,000 at peak.
  • Each device holds one open WebSocket. About 20 million open connections at peak; at 100,000 per gateway server, that is about 200 gateways.

Step 3: Design

Step 4: Send flow

  1. The sender's app sends a message with a client-generated ID (so retries do not duplicate it).
  2. The chat service assigns the next sequence number for the conversation and saves the message.
  3. The sender receives an acknowledgement ("sent").
  4. The event is published to Kafka with the conversation ID as the key, so order is kept.
  5. The registry finds the recipient's gateway and pushes the message. The recipient's app acknowledges, and the sender sees "delivered".
  6. If the recipient is offline, a push notification is sent. On reconnect, the app asks for messages after its last sequence number.
Key idea. Ordering comes from one sequence counter per conversation, not from device clocks. Clocks disagree; sequence numbers do not.

Step 5: Deep dives

  • Large groups: do not copy a message into 100,000 inboxes. Store it once and let readers pull from the conversation's log.
  • Presence: online status changes often. Broadcasting every change to every contact is too much. Show status only for people on screen, and use heartbeats that expire.
  • Gateway failure: clients reconnect elsewhere and resume from their last sequence number. Nothing is lost, because messages are saved before the acknowledgement.

Check yourself

  1. Where does message order come from, and why not from timestamps?
  2. Why does a client send its own message ID?
  3. How does a reconnecting phone catch up on missed messages?
