Lesson 20: News feed and fan-out

Goal

Decide when to do the work of building a feed: when a post is written, or when a feed is read.

The idea in plain words

Plain words. Imagine a newsletter. You can print a copy for every subscriber the moment an issue is ready (push), or you can keep one copy and have each reader collect the issues they follow when they visit (pull). Printing is fast to read but expensive when one author has a million subscribers. Pull is cheap to write but slow to read if a reader follows thousands of authors.

The two approaches

Push on write (fan-out)Pull on read
Cost of a new postCopy the post ID to every follower's timelineStore only once
Cost of opening the feedRead one precomputed list: fastMerge many authors at read time: slow
Breaks whenA celebrity has 100 million followersA user follows 5,000 accounts

The hybrid design

  1. Push the post ID into follower timelines when the author has fewer than a threshold of followers (for example, 10,000).
  2. For celebrities, do not push. When a user opens the feed, merge their precomputed timeline with the latest posts of the few celebrities they follow.
  3. Store IDs in timelines, not full posts. One post then serves millions of timelines, and an edit or delete is a single write.
  4. Paginate with a cursor (the last seen post's time and ID), not an offset, so new posts do not shift pages.
Key idea. The threshold is a tuning knob. Say what you would measure to set it: the number of followers at which push costs more than pull.
Common mistake. Designing one approach for all users. Real feeds have a very skewed follower distribution, which is why the hybrid exists.

Check yourself

  1. What is the main cost of push on write?
  2. Why store post IDs in timelines?
  3. Why paginate with a cursor instead of an offset?
Level: Intermediate · About 40 minutes

Lesson 21: Search and typeahead

Goal

Return the top suggestions for a prefix in under 100 ms, and explain how the data is built and updated.

The idea in plain words

Plain words. A dictionary with the most popular words printed first on each page. When you type "ca", you see the popular words that begin with "ca" immediately. Nobody searches the whole dictionary while you type.

How it is built

  1. Offline: a job reads query logs, counts each phrase, removes unsafe or rare phrases, and computes the top 10 phrases for every prefix (up to about 15 characters).
  2. Serve: store those lists in memory, sharded by the first characters of the prefix. A lookup is a direct read, not a search.
  3. Update: build a new version in the background, then swap the pointer. If the new version is bad, swap back.
  4. Fresh trends: a small real-time counter for the last hour is merged in at serve time.
Code (runs with Python 3, standard library only)
import math

class BloomFilter:
    def __init__(self, n_items: int, fp_rate: float = 0.01):
        self.m = int(-n_items * math.log(fp_rate) / (math.log(2) ** 2))  # bits
        self.k = max(1, round(self.m / n_items * math.log(2)))            # hash count
        self.bits = bytearray(self.m // 8 + 1)

    def _positions(self, item: str):
        d = hashlib.sha256(item.encode()).digest()
        a, b = int.from_bytes(d[:8], "big"), int.from_bytes(d[8:16], "big")
        return [(a + i * b) % self.m for i in range(self.k)]

    def add(self, item: str):
        for p in self._positions(item):
            self.bits[p // 8] |= 1 << (p % 8)

    def might_contain(self, item: str) -> bool:
        return all(self.bits[p // 8] & (1 << (p % 8)) for p in self._positions(item))

bf = BloomFilter(n_items=10000, fp_rate=0.01)
for i in range(10000):
    bf.add(f"item{i}")
print("all added items found (no false negatives):", all(bf.might_contain(f"item{i}") for i in range(10000)))
fp = sum(bf.might_contain(f"other{i}") for i in range(10000)) / 10000
print(f"false positive rate on 10,000 new items: {fp:.2%} (target 1%)")
print(f"bits per item: {bf.m/10000:.1f}, hash functions: {bf.k}")
Output when you run it:
all added items found (no false negatives): True
false positive rate on 10,000 new items: 1.04% (target 1%)
bits per item: 9.6, hash functions: 7
Key idea. Precompute the answer for every prefix. Typeahead is a read-heavy problem, so spend work offline to make each request a lookup.
Common mistake. Using "LIKE 'prefix%'" in a database on every keystroke. It sorts and scans per request and cannot rank cheaply at scale. Also, clients should debounce keystrokes (wait about 150 ms) to cut requests.

Check yourself

  1. Why precompute top suggestions for every prefix?
  2. How do you update suggestions without downtime?
  3. Why is debouncing on the client useful?
Level: Intermediate · About 50 minutes

Lesson 22: Ride matching with geographic cells

Goal

Find nearby drivers fast, match a rider to exactly one driver, and keep location data cheap.

The idea in plain words

Plain words. Cut the city map into a honeycomb of hexagons. To find a taxi, you look in your hexagon and the six around it. You never measure distances to every taxi in the city.

Step by step

  1. Each driver app sends its location every few seconds. Store only the latest location in memory, grouped by cell. Keep a sampled copy for analytics.
  2. A ride request searches the rider's cell and its neighbors.
  3. Rank candidates by road-network travel time (ETA), not straight-line distance. A river can make the straight line misleading.
  4. Offer the ride to the best driver with a 15-second timeout. If refused, offer to the next.
  5. When accepted, update the trip with a conditional write: "change state to matched only if still offered to this driver". Only one write can win.
Key idea. Two riders can request the same driver at the same time. The conditional write is what prevents double matching.
Common mistake. Writing every location update to a database. At a million updates per second, that is the bottleneck. Keep location in memory and treat it as disposable (drivers resend it every few seconds).

Check yourself

  1. Why search neighboring cells instead of all drivers?
  2. Why rank by road ETA instead of straight-line distance?
  3. What exact write prevents a driver from being matched twice?
Level: Intermediate to advanced · About 55 minutes

Lesson 23: Payments, where correctness comes first

Goal

Design a payment flow that never charges twice, never loses money, and always reconciles with the bank.

The idea in plain words

Plain words. A bank does not just store a number for your balance. Every movement of money is written as two entries: money leaves one account and enters another. The totals always balance. If they do not, someone made an error, and you can find it.

The state machine

Step by step

  1. The client sends a payment with an idempotency key (Lesson 16). A repeat returns the same result.
  2. The payment is saved as CREATED, with its version number. Each state change is a conditional update on the version.
  3. The payment processor is called with our payment ID as its idempotency key.
  4. If the processor times out, the outcome is unknown. Do not mark it failed. Ask the processor for the status first.
  5. On success, ledger entries are written in the same database transaction as the state change.
  6. Every night, reconciliation compares our records with the processor's settlement file. Mismatches go to a person.
Key idea. Use integers in minor units (cents or paise), never floating-point numbers, for money. Floats cause rounding errors.
Common mistake. Treating a timeout as a failure. The money may have moved. Unknown is a valid state, and it must be resolved, not guessed.

Check yourself

  1. Why must each state change check a version number?
  2. What do you do when the processor times out?
  3. Why store amounts as integers?
Level: Intermediate · About 45 minutes

Lesson 24: File storage and duplicate detection

Goal

Store large files efficiently, sync only what changed, and detect duplicates quickly.

The idea in plain words

Plain words. Imagine a 500-page book. If you fix one typo, you do not need to reprint the whole book; you replace the one page. Splitting files into chunks does the same: only changed chunks are uploaded.

Chunks and content addresses

  • Split each file into chunks (about 4 MB). Name each chunk by its hash. Two identical chunks are stored once.
  • A file version is a list of chunk hashes (a manifest).
  • Use content-defined chunk boundaries, so inserting text at the start only changes nearby chunks.

Commit safely

  1. The client sends the chunk hashes. The server replies with the ones it does not have.
  2. The client uploads only the missing chunks.
  3. The client commits the new manifest with the version it started from. If another device changed the file first, the commit fails, and the client saves a conflict copy instead of overwriting.

Duplicate detection with a Bloom filter

A Bloom filter answers "have I seen this?" with very little memory. It never says no when the answer is yes. A "maybe" is checked against the real store. Crawlers and caches use this to skip work.

Key idea. Commit metadata only after the chunks exist. A manifest that points to missing chunks is a corruption.

Check yourself

  1. Why is content-defined chunking better than fixed-size chunks for edited files?
  2. What happens when two devices edit the same file?
  3. Can a Bloom filter report an item that was never added? Can it miss one that was?
Level: Intermediate to advanced · About 45 minutes

Lesson 25: Metrics and analytics storage

Goal

Store millions of time-stamped numbers per second, compress them, and keep old data cheaply by downsampling.

The idea in plain words

Plain words. A weather station records the temperature every second. For last week's chart, you do not need every second; one reading per hour is enough. Keep detail for recent days, and summaries for older years.

The key ideas

  • Series: one metric plus its labels (for example, CPU on host 17 in region eu). Limit labels to a bounded set, such as service and region. Never use a user ID as a label, because the number of series explodes.
  • Compression: timestamps arrive at regular intervals, so store the change in the change. Float values are stored as the XOR of consecutive values. Together, this takes a couple of bytes per point.
  • Downsampling: keep raw points for 7 days, one-minute summaries for 90 days, one-hour summaries for 2 years. Store min, max, sum, and count so averages stay correct.
  • Percentiles cannot be averaged across hosts. Use histograms or sketches instead.
Common mistake. Averaging averages. An average of hourly averages is not the true average when hours have different numbers of events.

Check yourself

  1. Why must you never use a user ID as a metric label?
  2. Why store min, max, sum, and count in summaries?
  3. When would you choose Kappa over Lambda?
Level: Intermediate · About 45 minutes

Lesson 26: Video streaming and the CDN

Goal

Explain how an uploaded video becomes a stream that plays smoothly on a slow phone, and why most of the work happens at the network edge.

The idea in plain words

Plain words. A film is cut into short pieces, each available in several quality levels. Your player picks the quality for the next piece based on how fast your connection is right now. That is adaptive bitrate (ABR).

From upload to playback

  1. The upload goes straight to object storage in resumable parts.
  2. Transcoding workers create several resolutions and codecs, in parallel chunks.
  3. Each rendition is cut into segments of 2 to 6 seconds, with a manifest that lists them.
  4. The CDN caches segments close to viewers. Popular videos are served almost entirely from the edge.
  5. The player downloads a manifest, then fetches segments and switches quality as needed.
Key idea. Bandwidth is the main cost. The CDN hit ratio is the metric that matters most. Origin shielding stops a newly viral video from overwhelming storage.
Common mistake. Serving the original file. Devices and networks vary too much; you need several renditions.

Views count without slowing playback

Do not write one database row per view: at a billion views a day, that is about 11,500 writes per second. Clients batch view events; a stream job aggregates them per minute; the total is written periodically. Displayed counts can be rounded ("1.2M").

Check yourself

  1. What does adaptive bitrate choose, and based on what?
  2. What is origin shielding for?
  3. Why aggregate view counts instead of writing each view?
Level: Intermediate to advanced · About 45 minutes

Lesson 27: Job schedulers and workflows

Goal

Run jobs at a set time, retry them safely, and manage long multi-step workflows that survive crashes.

The idea in plain words

Plain words. A hospital ward has a list of tasks with times. A nurse "claims" a task by writing their name on it for 10 minutes. If the nurse collapses, the claim expires and another nurse takes over. The task must be safe to do twice, in case the first nurse was just slow.

How claiming works

  1. The scheduler finds jobs that are due and not claimed.
  2. A worker claims a job with a lease (an owner and an expiry time). The claim is atomic.
  3. The worker sends heartbeats to extend the lease while it works.
  4. If the worker dies, the lease expires and another worker can claim the job.
  5. Each claim gets a higher version number, which the job's side effects can check (fencing).
Key idea. Expect at-least-once execution. Make job handlers idempotent, and use the version number to reject work from an old claim.

Durable workflows

A long workflow (for example, "onboard a customer over 7 days") cannot live in one worker's memory. Durable execution engines (such as Temporal) record every step in a history. After a crash, another worker replays the history to rebuild the state. The workflow code must be deterministic: no direct random numbers or current-time calls; use the engine's versions.

Common mistake. Scheduling every job on one cron server. It is a single point of failure, with no retries and no visibility.

Check yourself

  1. What happens to a job when its worker dies mid-run?
  2. Why must handlers be idempotent?
  3. Why can a durable workflow survive a crash?
PART 5 · ADVANCED

Architecture and Operations

How large systems are organised, observed, secured, deployed, and kept alive across regions.

  • Lesson 28: Architecture styles and when to split a system
  • Lesson 29: CQRS and event sourcing
  • Lesson 30: Observability and SLOs
  • Lesson 31: Safe deployment
  • Lesson 32: Security in design
  • Lesson 33: Multi-region and disaster recovery
Level: Advanced · About 40 minutes

Lesson 28: Architecture styles and when to split a system

Goal

Choose between a monolith, services, and event-driven parts, and justify the choice with team and load facts.

The idea in plain words

Plain words. A single kitchen can cook for a family; a restaurant chain needs separate kitchens. Splitting a kitchen too early means more couriers, more coordination, and more things that go wrong. Split when a real limit forces you to, not because it looks modern.

Comparing styles

StyleGood whenCosts
Modular monolithSmall team, one deploy, shared dataDiscipline needed to keep modules apart
ServicesTeams must ship independently; parts scale differentlyNetwork failures, tracing, data ownership, versioning
Event-drivenMany consumers react to one fact; loose coupling mattersHarder to trace flows; eventual consistency

Steps to decide

  1. Name the team sizes and how often each part must deploy alone.
  2. Name the parts whose load differs by 10x or more (for example, search vs checkout).
  3. Draw data ownership: each piece of data has one owner that writes it.
  4. Only then split. Start with a modular monolith when unsure, and cut along the module boundaries later.
Key idea. Services are split by data ownership and team boundaries, not by technical layers ("a database service", "a validation service").
Common mistake. Starting with twenty microservices for a product with five engineers. Each service needs its own deploy, monitoring, and on-call.

Check yourself

  1. What is a good reason to split a system into services?
  2. What should be the unit of service ownership?
  3. Why start with a modular monolith when unsure?
Level: Advanced · About 50 minutes

Lesson 29: CQRS and event sourcing

Goal

Separate writes from reads when they need different shapes, and store changes as a history when auditing or replay matters.

The idea in plain words

Plain words. A bank statement is a list of every transaction. Your balance is a summary computed from that list. Event sourcing stores the list (the truth). CQRS keeps a separate summary for quick reading, updated from the list.

Steps

  1. A command ("withdraw 50") is validated against the current state.
  2. If valid, an event ("withdrawn 50, at version 7") is appended to the log, guarded by the expected version.
  3. Projections read the log and update read models (for example, a balance table or a search index).
  4. Snapshots every 1,000 events keep rebuilding fast.
Key idea. Read models are disposable. If one is wrong, delete it and rebuild it from the log.
Common mistake. Using event sourcing for everything. Most CRUD data does not need a history, and the extra complexity is real. Use it where audit, replay, or time-travel queries are core.

Check yourself

  1. What is the source of truth in event sourcing?
  2. Why is a read model safe to delete?
  3. Why guard appends with an expected version?
Level: Advanced · About 45 minutes

Lesson 30: Observability and SLOs

Goal

Measure what users feel, alert on it early, and decide when to spend reliability budget on new features.

The idea in plain words

Plain words. A car dashboard shows speed, fuel, and warning lights, so you know the car is fine before it stops. Observability is that dashboard for software. An SLO is the promise you make: "99.9% of requests succeed within 300 ms".

The three signals

  • Metrics: numbers over time (request rate, error rate, latency percentiles).
  • Logs: detailed events, searchable by request ID.
  • Traces: one request's path across services, with timings for each hop.

Error budget

A 99.9% monthly SLO allows about 43 minutes of failure per 30 days. That is the error budget. If it is spent, freeze risky releases. If plenty remains, ship faster.

Burn-rate alerts

Alert when the budget is burning fast, for example if 2% of it is gone in one hour. A single short spike does not wake anyone; a sustained burn does.

Key idea. Use percentiles (p95, p99), not averages. An average hides the slow tail that real users hit.
Common mistake. Alerting on CPU. Users do not feel CPU; they feel slow or failed requests. Alert on symptoms, and use CPU for diagnosis.

Check yourself

  1. How many minutes of failure does 99.9% allow in 30 days?
  2. What should trigger a page to an engineer?
  3. Why are percentiles better than averages for latency?
Level: Advanced · About 40 minutes

Lesson 31: Safe deployment

Goal

Ship changes to millions of users without outages, and roll back quickly when something goes wrong.

The idea in plain words

Plain words. Before you sell a new recipe to the whole restaurant, you serve it to one table. If the table is happy, you serve more tables. If something goes wrong, only one table noticed.

Strategies

StrategyHow it worksTrade-off
CanarySend 1%, then 10%, then 100% of traffic to the new versionNeeds good metrics to judge the canary
Blue-greenRun two full copies; switch traffic at onceDouble the capacity during the switch
RollingReplace instances a few at a timeOld and new versions run together

Database changes: expand and contract

  1. Expand: add the new column or table; write to both old and new.
  2. Migrate: backfill old rows in small batches.
  3. Switch: read from the new place.
  4. Contract: remove the old column, only after a full release cycle.
Key idea. Every change must be compatible with the version before and after it. Old and new code run side by side during a rollout.
Common mistake. Renaming a column in one deploy. The old code still reads the old name, and the rollout fails.

Check yourself

  1. What does a canary test that a blue-green deploy does not?
  2. Why is expand-contract needed for schema changes?
  3. Why must old and new code work together?
Level: Advanced · About 40 minutes

Lesson 32: Security in design

Goal

Design authentication, authorization, and data protection into the system from the start, and name the common attacks.

The idea in plain words

Plain words. Authentication asks "who are you?" (a badge at the door). Authorization asks "may you enter this room?" (the badge must open that door). Many breaches happen because the badge works everywhere.

Core pieces

  • Login: OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect hand users to an identity provider. Your service receives a short-lived token.
  • Tokens: JWTs are signed, so services verify them without a call. Keep them short-lived (minutes) and revoke via refresh tokens.
  • Service to service: mutual TLS, where both sides present certificates.
  • Secrets: stored in a secrets manager, rotated, never in code.
  • Data: encrypt in transit (TLS) and at rest; keep personal data minimal.

Attacks to design against

  • IDOR: changing /orders/123 to /orders/124 and seeing someone else's order. Check ownership on every object access.
  • Rate abuse: limit logins and expensive endpoints (Lesson 13).
  • Injection: never build SQL by joining strings; use parameters.
Key idea. Authorize every object access, not just the entry point. Most real breaches are "logged in but allowed to see too much".

Check yourself

  1. What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
  2. Why keep JWTs short-lived?
  3. What is IDOR, and how do you prevent it?
Level: Advanced · About 50 minutes

Lesson 33: Multi-region and disaster recovery

Goal

Keep the system running when a whole region fails, and state the recovery time and data loss you accept.

The idea in plain words

Plain words. A company keeps a copy of its records in a second city. If the first office burns, the second one opens. The question is how long the move takes (RTO) and how many recent records might be lost (RPO).

Patterns

PatternRTORPOCost
Backup and restoreHoursHoursLow
Warm standbyMinutesSeconds to minutesMedium
Active-activeNear zeroNear zeroHigh, and conflicts to solve

Steps

  1. Write down RTO and RPO per service. Not every service needs the same.
  2. Choose the pattern that meets them at the lowest cost.
  3. Replicate data across regions; accept asynchronous lag if RPO allows it.
  4. Route users with DNS or a global load balancer; test failover regularly.
  5. Keep state for each user in one home region to avoid conflicting writes.
Key idea. A disaster plan that has never been rehearsed is a guess. Practice failover on a schedule.
Common mistake. Active-active writes to the same record in two regions without a conflict rule. Two regions can accept contradictory updates.

Check yourself

  1. What does RPO measure?
  2. When is warm standby better than active-active?
  3. Why give each user a home region?
PART 6 · LOW-LEVEL DESIGN

Object-Oriented Design

Classes, patterns, and concurrency, applied to classic interview problems. Every coded example in this part was run and its output checked.

  • Lesson 34: Design principles (SOLID) and a method
  • Lesson 35: Patterns you will actually use
  • Lesson 36: Concurrency in LLD
  • Lesson 37: Parking lot
  • Lesson 38: LRU cache
  • Lesson 39: Vending machine and elevator (state)
  • Lesson 40: Splitwise (debt simplification)
  • Lesson 41: Movie ticket booking
Level: Beginner to intermediate · About 40 minutes

Lesson 34: Design principles (SOLID) and a method

Goal

Turn a vague problem into classes using a fixed method, and check the result against five principles.

The method, step by step

  1. Clarify (3 minutes): ask about actors, actions, scale of one machine, concurrency, and what is out of scope. Write the answers down.
  2. List nouns and verbs: nouns become classes (Vehicle, Spot, Ticket). Verbs become methods (park, leave). Adjectives become fields or enums (size, status).
  3. Relationships: "has a" is composition (a Lot has Spots). "is a" is inheritance (a Truck is a Vehicle), and you should use it sparingly.
  4. Name the varying behaviour: pricing, eviction, seat selection. These become interfaces or strategy objects.
  5. Walk one scenario end to end against your classes. Most design bugs show up here.
  6. Handle concurrency and failure last, but say you will.

SOLID in plain words

LetterPrinciplePlain wordsParking lot example
SSingle responsibilityOne reason to changePricing is not inside Vehicle
OOpen/closedAdd behaviour by adding a classAdd a weekend price class; no edit to the lot
LLiskov substitutionA subtype can replace its parentAny Vehicle subtype can be parked and charged
IInterface segregationSmall, focused interfacesGate reader does not need payment methods
DDependency inversionDepend on interfaces, not concrete classesLot takes any pricing function, not a fixed rate table

Worked example: the question "should this be inheritance?"

Suppose you start with a class hierarchy: Car, Truck, Bike, each with its own fee method. Now the business adds "electric car at a discount". You must edit the Car class, and every new rule adds a branch or a subclass. Instead, keep the vehicle a simple data object and pass the pricing rule in. Adding a rule then adds one function and no edits to existing code. This is the open/closed principle in practice.

Interview follow-ups

  • "Why not inheritance for vehicles?" Vehicles differ by size, not by behaviour. A size field plus a pricing strategy is simpler.
  • "How do you test this?" Inject the pricing function and the clock. Then a test controls both.
Key idea. Prefer composition over inheritance. Keep rules you expect to change behind an interface.
Common mistake. Typing code before clarifying. Ten minutes of questions saves thirty minutes of rewrites.

Check yourself

  1. What do nouns, verbs, and adjectives become?
  2. Which principle is broken if adding a discount requires editing Car?
  3. Name the three things you would clarify before designing a parking lot.
Level: Intermediate · About 45 minutes

Lesson 35: Patterns you will actually use

Goal

Recognise the few patterns that show up in most interview problems, and know the signal that calls for each.

The idea in plain words

Plain words. A pattern is a named shape you have seen before. Strategy is "swap the rule without touching the user". State is "the same button does different things in different modes". Name the pattern only after you have the shape in mind.

The patterns, with their signals

PatternSignal in the problemExample
Strategy"Rules vary" or "algorithm can change"Pricing, eviction policy, seat ranking
State"Behaviour depends on the current mode"Vending machine, elevator, order status
Observer"When X happens, notify several parties"Booking confirmation to email, SMS, app
Factory"Create the right subtype from a input"Vehicle types from a request
Command"Undo", "queue", or "log actions"Text editor undo, job queue
Chain of responsibility"Each handler may pass the request on"Support escalation levels

Strategy vs State, the most common confusion

Both swap an object's behaviour. The difference is who decides the swap. With Strategy, the caller picks the algorithm (the customer chooses a discount rule). With State, the object changes its own behaviour as events happen (a vending machine moves from Idle to HasMoney after a coin). If the object transitions itself, use State.

Interview follow-ups

  • "Is this over-engineered?" If there are only two cases, use a plain if statement and say so. Patterns earn their place when a third case is likely.
  • "How do you add a new case?" Show that the pattern adds one class and touches nothing else.
Key idea. In an interview, explain why a pattern fits: "I used Strategy so pricing can change without editing booking." A name alone earns little credit.
Common mistake. Forcing a pattern where a simple condition is clearer.

Check yourself

  1. What is the difference between Strategy and State in who decides the change?
  2. Which pattern lets you undo actions?
  3. When is a plain if statement the better choice?
Level: Intermediate to advanced · About 45 minutes

Lesson 36: Concurrency in LLD

Goal

Make shared state safe when many threads act at once, while keeping the locked part as small as possible.

The idea in plain words

Plain words. Two people reach for the last seat in a cinema. Each checks "is it free?" and sees yes. Both sit down. The check and the sit must be one indivisible step, or someone else slips in between. This is a check-then-act race.

Tools and when to use them

  • Lock around exactly the check-and-act pair. Keep the critical section short: no network calls or printing inside the lock.
  • Conditional update (compare-and-set): "set to booked only if still free". This is the database version of the same idea.
  • Single-flight: when many threads ask for the same missing value, compute it once and share the result.
  • Immutable objects: nothing to protect when nothing changes.

Worked example: why the lock must cover both steps

If you check availability under a lock but mark the seat outside it, a second thread can pass the check between your two steps. The rule: the lock must cover the read and the write together.

Interview follow-ups

  • "Why not lock the whole system?" It serialises every request and removes the point of concurrency. Lock per resource where you can.
  • "What about deadlock?" Acquire locks in a fixed order, and keep each critical section to one lock where possible.
Key idea. Name the shared state and the check-then-act pair. Lock exactly that.
Common mistake. Locking around a slow external call, which turns a fast system into a queue.

Check yourself

  1. What is a check-then-act race?
  2. Why must the lock cover both the read and the write?
  3. How would you avoid deadlock when locking two resources?
Level: Beginner to intermediate · About 60 minutes

Lesson 37: Parking lot

Goal

Design a parking lot with several vehicle sizes, pricing, and safe concurrent entry, and run it.

Step 1: Clarify

  • Vehicle types: bike, car, truck. Can a truck use a car spot? Assume a bigger spot can take a smaller vehicle.
  • Pricing: per hour, rounded up. Can pricing change by time of day? (We will allow it through a strategy.)
  • Entrances and exits: several gates, one ticket per entry, one exit payment.
  • When full: reject the entry with a clear reason.

Step 2: Classes and relationships

ClassResponsibility
VehicleTypeThe kinds of vehicle and which spot sizes fit them
SpotOne space with a size and free flag
ParkingLotOwns spots, issues tickets, enforces the lock
Pricing (function or strategy)Turns vehicle type and duration into a fee

Step 3: Allocation and concurrency

Keep free spots in a list per size. Assigning a spot removes it from the list, which is a check-then-act step. One lock around park and leave makes it safe (Lesson 36). Pick the smallest fitting size first, so trucks are not blocked by bikes parking in big spaces.

Step 4: The code (verified)

class VehicleType(Enum):
    BIKE = 1; CAR = 2; TRUCK = 3

class Spot:
    def __init__(self, sid, size):
        self.id, self.size, self.free = sid, size, True

class ParkingLot:
    """Allocation is guarded by one lock: check-then-act must be atomic."""
    FIT = {VehicleType.BIKE: (1, 2, 3), VehicleType.CAR: (2, 3), VehicleType.TRUCK: (3,)}
    def __init__(self, spots, pricing):
        self._lock = threading.Lock()
        self._free = {s: [] for s in (1, 2, 3)}
        self._tickets = {}
        self._pricing = pricing          # Strategy: callable(vtype, minutes) -> cents
        for sp in spots:
            self._free[sp.size].append(sp)
    def park(self, vtype, ticket_id, now):
        with self._lock:
            for size in self.FIT[vtype]:           # smallest fitting spot first
                if self._free[size]:
                    spot = self._free[size].pop()
                    self._tickets[ticket_id] = (spot, vtype, now)
                    return spot.id
            raise RuntimeError("no spot available")
    def leave(self, ticket_id, now):
        with self._lock:
            spot, vtype, start = self._tickets.pop(ticket_id)
            self._free[spot.size].append(spot)
            minutes = max(1, -(-(now - start) // 60))     # round up to whole minutes
            return self._pricing(vtype, minutes)

def hourly(vtype, minutes):
    rate = {VehicleType.BIKE: 20, VehicleType.CAR: 50, VehicleType.TRUCK: 120}[vtype]  # cents/hour
    return rate * -(-minutes // 60)

lot = ParkingLot([Spot(1,1), Spot(2,2), Spot(3,3), Spot(4,2)], hourly)
print("car ->", lot.park(VehicleType.CAR, "T1", 0))
print("truck ->", lot.park(VehicleType.TRUCK, "T2", 0))
print("fee for T1 after 150 min (cents):", lot.leave("T1", 150*60))
try:
    lot.park(VehicleType.TRUCK, "T3", 0)
except RuntimeError as e:
    print("truck again ->", e)

Step 5: Output from the run

car -> 4
truck -> 3
fee for T1 after 150 min (cents): 150
truck again -> no spot available

Step 6: Walk one scenario by hand

A car arrives at time 0 and takes spot 4 (a size 2 spot). It leaves after 150 minutes. Duration rounds up to 150 minutes, which is 3 billed hours at 50 cents each, so the fee is 150 cents. Spot 4 returns to the free list. A truck arriving next finds size 3 spot 3 free and takes it.

Interview follow-ups

  • "Add EV charging spots." Add a flag on Spot and a filter on allocation. The pricing does not change.
  • "Add weekend pricing." Pass a different pricing function. Nothing else changes (Lesson 34).
  • "What if the lot is distributed across floors?" Track free spots per floor and per size, and choose a floor first.
  • "How do you avoid two cars getting the same spot?" The lock. Explain why check-then-act needs both steps inside it.
Key idea. Keep allocation separate from pricing. Changing the price rule must not touch spot assignment.
Common mistake. Putting fee logic inside Vehicle. A vehicle should not know how the lot charges.

Check yourself

  1. Which class should own pricing, and why?
  2. Why does the code pick the smallest fitting spot first?
  3. How would you add EV charging without changing pricing?
Level: Intermediate · About 50 minutes

Lesson 38: LRU cache

Goal

Build a cache that evicts the least recently used item, with get and put in constant time, and explain the structure behind it.

The idea in plain words

Plain words. A desk with room for five books. When you pick a book up, you put it on top. When a sixth book arrives, you remove the one that has sat at the bottom the longest.

Why two structures

  • A hash map gives O(1) lookup of a key.
  • A doubly linked list gives O(1) move-to-front and O(1) removal, because each node knows its neighbours.
  • Together: the map finds the node, the list orders it. Neither alone is enough: a map cannot tell recency, and a list cannot find a key quickly.

Step by step

  1. get(k): if missing, return nothing. If present, move its node to the front and return the value.
  2. put(k, v): if present, update and move to front. Otherwise insert at the front; if over capacity, remove the tail node and delete its key from the map.

Code (verified)

Python's OrderedDict is a hash map with a linked list inside, so it does both jobs. In an interview, say so, then describe the two-structure version on the whiteboard.

class LRUCache:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.cap = capacity
        self.d = OrderedDict()          # key -> value; order = recency
        self.lock = threading.Lock()
    def get(self, key):
        with self.lock:
            if key not in self.d:
                return None
            self.d.move_to_end(key)     # most recent at the end
            return self.d[key]
    def put(self, key, value):
        with self.lock:
            if key in self.d:
                self.d.move_to_end(key)
            self.d[key] = value
            if len(self.d) > self.cap:
                self.d.popitem(last=False)   # evict least recent

c = LRUCache(2)
c.put("a", 1); c.put("b", 2)
c.get("a")                 # a is now most recent
c.put("c", 3)              # evicts b
print("LRU get b ->", c.get("b"), "| get a ->", c.get("a"), "| get c ->", c.get("c"))

Output from the run

LRU get b -> None | get a -> 1 | get c -> 3

Walk one scenario by hand

Capacity 2. put a, put b: order is b (newest), a. get a: order becomes a, b. put c: capacity exceeded, so the least recent, b, is evicted. get b misses. That is exactly the printed result.

Interview follow-ups

  • "Make it thread-safe." One lock around get and put, since both reorder the list. Note that get writes too, so a read-write lock does not help here.
  • "Add a TTL." Store the expiry with each value and check it on get; a background sweep removes old entries.
  • "Why not a plain dictionary with timestamps?" Finding the least recent entry would need a scan of all entries, which is O(n) per eviction.
Key idea. The map finds, the list orders. Each structure does one job, and both are O(1).
Common mistake. Forgetting to delete the evicted key from the map, so the cache reports a value it no longer holds.

Check yourself

  1. Why is a doubly linked list needed rather than a singly linked one?
  2. What happens on a get that misses?
  3. Why does a read-write lock not help in this design?
Level: Intermediate · About 55 minutes

Lesson 39: Vending machine and elevator (state)

Goal

Model a machine whose buttons mean different things in different states, using the State pattern, and reason about the elevator's choice of car.

The idea in plain words

Plain words. Press a product button before inserting money and nothing happens. Insert money and the same button now dispenses. The button did not change; the state did.

Step by step: vending machine

  1. States: Idle, HasMoney. (Add Dispensing and OutOfStock in a fuller design.)
  2. Every state implements the same actions: insert, select. Actions a state does not allow raise an error.
  3. Transitions happen inside the states: Idle moves to HasMoney after a coin; HasMoney moves to Idle after a sale.
  4. Stock and credit live in the machine. States only decide what is allowed.

Code (verified)

class State:
    def insert(self, m, coin): raise RuntimeError("not allowed now")
    def select(self, m, code): raise RuntimeError("not allowed now")
class Idle(State):
    def insert(self, m, coin):
        m.credit += coin; m.state = HasMoney()
class HasMoney(State):
    def insert(self, m, coin): m.credit += coin
    def select(self, m, code):
        price = m.stock[code][1]
        if m.stock[code][0] == 0: raise RuntimeError("sold out")
        if m.credit < price: raise RuntimeError(f"need {price - m.credit} more")
        m.stock[code][0] -= 1; m.credit -= price
        m.state = Idle()
        return f"dispensed {code}, change {m.credit}"
class Machine:
    def __init__(self, stock):
        self.stock, self.credit, self.state = stock, 0, Idle()
    def insert(self, coin): self.state.insert(self, coin)
    def select(self, code): return self.state.select(self, code)

vm = Machine({"A1": [1, 150]})
print("select before coin ->", end=" ")
try: vm.select("A1")
except RuntimeError as e: print(e)
vm.insert(100); print("insert 100 ->", vm.state.__class__.__name__)
try: vm.select("A1")
except RuntimeError as e: print("select ->", e)
vm.insert(100)
print(vm.select("A1"))

Output from the run

select before coin -> not allowed now
insert 100 -> HasMoney
select -> need 50 more
dispensed A1, change 50

Elevator: the decision

For a new hall call, score each car. A car that is idle costs its distance to the floor. A car moving toward the floor in the same direction, and not yet past it, costs the same distance. A car moving the other way costs the distance plus a penalty, because it must finish its run first. Assign the request to the lowest score. Keep stops in sorted sets so the car serves them in order.

Interview follow-ups

  • "Add an OutOfStock state." Add one class. The transitions into it are the only edits.
  • "Why not one if-else on a state string?" Each new state touches every method. The State pattern confines the change to one class.
  • "How do elevators avoid starvation?" Serve requests in the chosen direction first, then reverse (the SCAN algorithm). A request that waits too long can get a priority boost.
Key idea. Each state decides what is allowed; the context holds the data.
Common mistake. A long if-else on a state string spread across methods. It is the same bug as an unclear state machine in production.

Check yourself

  1. What does the State pattern change at runtime?
  2. Where should stock be stored, and why?
  3. Why does the elevator add a penalty for a car moving the wrong way?
Level: Intermediate · About 55 minutes

Lesson 40: Splitwise (debt simplification)

Goal

Record shared expenses and reduce many small debts to the fewest payments needed to settle everything.

The idea in plain words

Plain words. Ann is owed 20 and Ben owes Cara 20 and Ann owes Ben 20 in the same week. You do not need three payments. Netting shows that Cara can pay Ann directly, and Ben is out of it.

Step by step

  1. For each expense, add to the payer's balance and subtract each person's share. Work in integer cents.
  2. After all expenses, each person has one net number: positive means they are owed money, negative means they owe.
  3. Put creditors and debtors in two max-heaps, keyed by amount.
  4. Repeatedly pair the largest debtor with the largest creditor. Pay the smaller amount. Put back whoever still has a balance.
  5. Stop when one side is empty. The totals always match, because the balances sum to zero.

Worked example

Ann pays 30.00 for dinner shared by three (Ann, Ben, Cara), so each owes 10.00. Ben pays 6.00 for a drink shared by Ben and Cara, so each owes 3.00. Net balances: Ann paid 30.00 and owes 10.00, so she is owed 20.00. Ben paid 6.00 and owes 13.00, so he owes 7.00. Cara owes 13.00 and paid nothing, so she owes 13.00. Check: 20.00 minus 7.00 minus 13.00 is zero. Cara pays Ann 13.00 and Ben pays Ann 7.00: two payments, not four.

Code (verified)

def simplify(balances):
    """balances: name -> net cents (positive = is owed). Returns list of (payer, payee, cents)."""
    creditors = [[-v, k] for k, v in balances.items() if v > 0]  # heap of (-amount, name)
    debtors = [[v, k] for k, v in balances.items() if v < 0]
    heapq.heapify(creditors)
    heapq.heapify(debtors)
    payments = []
    while creditors and debtors:
        c_amt, c_name = heapq.heappop(creditors)
        d_amt, d_name = heapq.heappop(debtors)
        c_amt, d_amt = -c_amt, -d_amt
        pay = min(c_amt, d_amt)
        payments.append((d_name, c_name, pay))
        if c_amt - pay > 0: heapq.heappush(creditors, [-(c_amt - pay), c_name])
        if d_amt - pay > 0: heapq.heappush(debtors, [-(d_amt - pay), d_name])
    return payments

# Ann paid 3000 for dinner shared by 3 -> Ann +2000, Ben -1000, Cara -1000 ; Ben paid 600 for 2 (Ben, Cara) -> Ben +300, Cara -300
bal = {"Ann": 2000, "Ben": -1000 + 300, "Cara": -1000 - 300}
print("balances:", bal)
for d, c, amt in simplify(bal):
    print(f"{d} pays {c} {amt/100:.2f}")

Output from the run

balances: {'Ann': 2000, 'Ben': -700, 'Cara': -1300}
Cara pays Ann 13.00
Ben pays Ann 7.00

Interview follow-ups

  • "How many payments at most?" n minus 1 for n people with nonzero balances. Each payment settles at least one person fully.
  • "Why are the balances netted first?" Netting removes intermediate debts. Simplifying pairs before netting can produce more payments.
  • "Why integer cents?" Floating-point rounding can leave a balance of 0.01 that never clears (Lesson 23).
  • "Does this always give the minimum number of payments?" Finding the true minimum is NP-hard in general, so the greedy approach is the practical answer. Say so, and mention it is optimal in common cases.
Key idea. Work with net balances, not individual IOUs.
Common mistake. Using floating-point money.

Check yourself

  1. Why compute net balances first?
  2. What is the maximum number of payments for n people?
  3. Why is the greedy method acceptable even though the true minimum is hard?
Level: Intermediate to advanced · About 60 minutes

Lesson 41: Movie ticket booking

Goal

Let users pick seats for a show, hold them briefly, and confirm payment without double booking or stuck seats.

Step 1: Clarify

  • One show, many seats. Can a user pick seats across rows? Assume yes.
  • Hold duration: 5 minutes. A held seat is free again after expiry.
  • Payment fails or is late: the hold must not be confirmed after expiry.

Step 2: The seat state machine

Each seat is free, held (by one user, until a time), or booked. Only these transitions exist: free to held, held to booked, held to free (on expiry or cancel), and held to free when a hold expires. Booked is final.

Step 3: All-or-nothing holds

A user selecting A1, A2 and A3 must get all three or none. The hold checks every seat and then writes every seat, under one lock. A partial hold would leave the user with an unusable selection.

Step 4: Confirm only if the hold is still yours

Confirmation checks that the seat is still held by this user and has not expired. If the payment finishes late, the confirm fails, and the user must select again. This stops a slow payment from taking seats that someone else has since been offered.

Code (verified)

import time as _t
class Seats:
    def __init__(self):
        self.status = {}              # seat -> (state, holder, expires_at)
        self.lock = threading.Lock()
    def hold(self, seats, user, now, ttl=300):
        with self.lock:               # all-or-nothing for the request
            for s in seats:
                st, _, exp = self.status.get(s, ("free", None, 0))
                if st == "booked" or (st == "held" and exp > now):
                    raise RuntimeError(f"{s} unavailable")
            for s in seats:
                self.status[s] = ("held", user, now + ttl)
    def confirm(self, seats, user, now):
        with self.lock:
            for s in seats:
                st, holder, exp = self.status.get(s, ("free", None, 0))
                if not (st == "held" and holder == user and exp > now):
                    raise RuntimeError(f"hold on {s} expired or lost")
            for s in seats:
                self.status[s] = ("booked", user, None)

seats = Seats()
seats.hold(["A1", "A2"], "u1", now=0)
try: seats.hold(["A2", "A3"], "u2", now=10)
except RuntimeError as e: print("u2 hold ->", e)
try: seats.confirm(["A1", "A2"], "u1", now=400)
except RuntimeError as e: print("late confirm ->", e)
seats.hold(["A1", "A2"], "u1", now=400)
seats.confirm(["A1", "A2"], "u1", now=401)
print("A1 status ->", seats.status["A1"][0])

Output from the run

u2 hold -> A2 unavailable
late confirm -> hold on A1 expired or lost
A1 status -> booked

Interview follow-ups

  • "Where should holds live in production?" Not in process memory: a restart loses them. Use a database with conditional updates, or a store with TTLs (for example, Redis with expiry). Holds must survive a restart or the seats are lost.
  • "How do you scale to a blockbuster opening?" Partition by show, so each show's seats live on one shard. Expect hot spots and put a waiting room in front.
  • "Who releases expired holds?" A background job plus a check on every read. The check makes correctness independent of the job's timing.
Key idea. A hold is a lease with an expiry. It protects users from each other without locking seats forever.
Common mistake. Holding seats only in application memory.

Check yourself

  1. What makes a late payment unable to take seats from someone else?
  2. Why hold all the seats of one request together?
  3. Where should hold state live, and why not in memory?

Running the Interview

Level: All levels · About 40 minutes

Lesson 42: The 45-minute method, step by step

Goal

Run any system design interview with a clock, so you never run out of time in the middle of the design.

MinutesStepWhat you produce
0 to 5RequirementsTwo to three functional and two to three non-functional requirements; what is out of scope
5 to 8EstimatesQPS (average and peak), storage per year, bandwidth
8 to 12Core API and data modelEndpoints and the main tables or documents
12 to 25High-level designDiagram: clients, gateway, services, storage, queues, caches
25 to 40Deep divesTwo or three hard parts, chosen with the interviewer
40 to 45Wrap-upBottlenecks, failure handling, monitoring, next steps

Tips that matter

  • Say the time out loud at each step: "I have 5 minutes for estimates."
  • Ask one question, then wait. The interviewer's answer decides the design.
  • Draw as you talk. Label arrows with the protocol and the data.
  • Always end the high-level design with the question "where does this fail?"
Key idea. The deep dive is where you score. Pick the part with the most trade-offs (usually consistency, scale, or failure) and go deep.
Common mistake. Spending 25 minutes on requirements and estimates, then running out of time for the design.

Check yourself

  1. Which step gets the most time, and why?
  2. When does the interviewer's answer change your design?
  3. What must you say at the end of the high-level design?
Level: All levels · About 30 minutes

Lesson 43: Recovering from mistakes and pressure

Goal

Handle the moments when you are stuck, wrong, or interrupted, without losing the interviewer.

Common situations and responses

SituationSay or do
You don't know a technology"I haven't used it, but the problem needs X. Here is how I would reason about X." Then reason from first principles.
You made a mistake"I see a problem with what I drew: the cache can serve stale data. Here is the fix." Own it briefly and move on.
You are stuckList two options with one trade-off each, then pick one and say why.
The interviewer pushes back"That's a good point. What would you prefer?" Treat it as a request for a trade-off, not a verdict.
Plain words. Interviewers rarely care that you know every answer. They care whether you can reason in public, notice your own errors, and make a decision.
Key idea. Narrate your reasoning. A wrong idea that is clearly reasoned scores better than a silent guess.
Common mistake. Going silent when stuck. Silence looks like you have stopped working.

Check yourself

  1. What do you say when you don't know a technology?
  2. How do you respond to a challenge to your design?
  3. What should you do when stuck?
Level: All levels · About 45 minutes

Lesson 44: Your resume and behavioural stories

Goal

Turn your real project work into short stories you can tell with numbers, and connect each one to a design concept.

Use the STAR format

Situation, Task, Action, Result. Keep each part to one or two sentences. Spend most of the time on Action: the decisions you made and why.

Your stories, from your resume

ProjectDesign concept it showsNumber to state
Kafka to Druid pipelineStreaming ingestion, time-series storage1M+ events per day, sub-second queries
Temporal XML processingDurable workflows, retries1M+ files per day
Kafka to IcebergCompaction, deduplication, rollupLoad down 40%; up to 10x reduction
SQL query generation serviceCaching, query designReport time down 95%
Distributed cache (Node.js)Partitioning with consistent hashing, replication200 virtual nodes; zero invalidation
CamelThar (chat)Real-time delivery, caching50 ms chat; sub-10 ms cache hits
Check before any interview. Earlier, the LaTeX resume and the PDF showed different numbers. This course uses the PDF. Confirm each number, because an interviewer may ask how you measured it.
Key idea. Be ready to go one level deeper on any claim. "Why 200 virtual nodes?" is a likely question; answer with the trade-off of balance versus memory.

Check yourself

  1. What are the four parts of a STAR story?
  2. Which part should get the most time?
  3. Pick one resume project and link it to a design concept from this course.
Level: Beginner, intermediate, advanced · About 60 minutes

Lesson 45: Mock interviews for each level

Goal

Practise full interviews at your level, and score yourself honestly.

Beginner mock: URL shortener

  1. Requirements: shorten a URL, redirect, 100M new links a year, redirects fast.
  2. Estimate: writes about 3 per second; reads about 300 per second at peak; storage a few hundred GB over five years.
  3. API: POST /links, GET /{code}. Table: code, long URL, owner, created time.
  4. High level: stateless service, key-value store, cache for hot codes (Lesson 6).
  5. Deep dive: how codes are generated without collisions (Lesson 7, Snowflake or base62 counter).

Intermediate mock: chat system

  1. Requirements: one-to-one and group chats, online status, message history, delivery guarantees.
  2. Estimate: a few million concurrent connections; write rate of messages per second.
  3. High level: gateway with WebSocket connections, message service, storage partitioned by conversation, queue for fan-out.
  4. Deep dive: ordering inside a conversation, and at-least-once delivery with idempotent clients (Lesson 16).

Advanced mock: payments platform

  1. Requirements: charge once, refunds, reconciliation with the bank, 99.99% availability.
  2. High level: API, payment state machine (Lesson 23), ledger, processor adapters, outbox to events.
  3. Deep dive: a processor timeout, and how reconciliation finds the missing money.
  4. Wrap-up: multi-region plan with RTO and RPO stated (Lesson 33).
Key idea. Record each mock. Time yourself, then compare with the answer in the appendix.

Check yourself

  1. Which part of the advanced mock is most likely to be asked in depth?
  2. How many estimates do you need before the design?
  3. What did you miss in your last mock?
Level: All levels · About 30 minutes

Check yourself

APPENDIX

Answers, Cheat Sheets, and Glossary

Use this section after each lesson's Check yourself, and during revision.

  • Answer key for every Check yourself

Reference

Appendix A: Answer key

Try each question before reading the answer. Answers are short; the lesson gives the full reasoning.

Lessons 1 to 7

  1. Clarify requirements and estimates first, then design, then deep dive (Lesson 1).
  2. A request passes DNS, load balancer, stateless service, then storage (Lesson 2).
  3. Average QPS = daily actions divided by 86,400; peak is two to three times average (Lesson 4).
  4. B-trees are read-friendly; LSM trees are write-friendly. A composite index helps queries on its left-most columns (Lessons 5, 8).
  5. Cache-aside, expire on write; with hit ratio h, average latency is h times the cache time plus (1 minus h) times the database time (Lesson 6).

Lessons 8 to 19

  1. Leader-follower replication is simple; sync gives safety, async gives speed (Lesson 8).
  2. Consistent hashing with virtual nodes keeps moves small when servers change (Lesson 9).
  3. Quorum reads and writes overlap when R + W is greater than N (Lesson 10).
  4. Serializable isolation prevents write skew (Lesson 11).
  5. Queues deliver work once; logs keep history for replay (Lesson 12).
  6. Token bucket allows bursts up to capacity and refills at a steady rate (Lesson 13).
  7. Raft commits when a majority acknowledges; fencing tokens reject stale leaders (Lessons 14, 15).
  8. Full jitter spreads retries so they do not arrive together (Lesson 15).
  9. Open circuit fails fast; half-open lets a few probes through (Lesson 15).
  10. Idempotency keys make repeats safe (Lesson 16).
  11. Outbox writes the event in the same transaction as the state change (Lesson 16).
  12. Saga compensations undo completed steps when a later step fails (Lesson 16).
  13. Partition by key for order; the consumer group shares partitions (Lesson 17).
  14. Watermarks tell the system when a window is complete enough to emit (Lesson 18).

Lessons 20 to 33

  1. Push normal posts; pull celebrity posts at read time (Lesson 20).
  2. Precompute top suggestions per prefix; swap versions without downtime (Lesson 21).
  3. Search neighboring cells; rank by road ETA; conditional write to match (Lesson 22).
  4. Version checks on state changes; treat timeouts as unknown; integer amounts (Lesson 23).
  5. Content-defined chunks; commit the manifest after chunks exist (Lesson 24).
  6. Never use user IDs as labels; downsample with min, max, sum, count (Lesson 25).
  7. ABR picks quality from current bandwidth; origin shielding protects storage (Lesson 26).
  8. A lease expires if the worker dies; handlers must be idempotent (Lesson 27).
  9. Split by data ownership and team boundaries; start modular (Lesson 28).
  10. The event log is the truth; read models can be rebuilt (Lesson 29).
  11. 99.9% over 30 days allows about 43 minutes of failure (Lesson 30).
  12. Canary tests with real traffic; expand-contract for schema changes (Lesson 31).
  13. Authentication says who; authorization says what; check ownership on each object (Lesson 32).
  14. RPO is how much recent data you may lose; warm standby balances cost and recovery (Lesson 33).

Lessons 34 to 46

  1. Nouns become classes; verbs become methods; depend on interfaces (Lesson 34).
  2. State changes behaviour at runtime; Strategy swaps a rule (Lesson 35).
  3. Check-then-act races need one atomic step or a lock (Lesson 36).
  4. Pricing belongs to a strategy, outside the Vehicle (Lesson 37).
  5. Doubly linked list gives O(1) move and removal (Lesson 38).
  6. Stock lives in the machine; states decide what is allowed (Lesson 39).
  7. Net balances give at most n minus one payments (Lesson 40).
  8. A hold is a lease with an expiry (Lesson 41).
  9. Spend most time on the high-level design and deep dives (Lesson 42).
  10. Narrate reasoning; own mistakes briefly (Lesson 43).
  11. STAR: Situation, Task, Action, Result; Action gets most time (Lesson 44).
  12. The advanced payments mock: deep dive on timeouts and reconciliation (Lesson 45).
  13. Revisit the lesson for any row marked "not yet" (Lesson 46).

Seconds per day86,400 (round to 10^5 for quick math)

Peak QPS2 to 3 times average
Availability 99.9%about 43 minutes per 30 days; 8.8 hours per year
Availability 99.99%about 4.3 minutes per 30 days; 52 minutes per year
Cache average latencyh × t_cache + (1 − h) × t_db

Appendix C: Glossary

TermMeaning
Cache-asideApp reads the cache, falls back to the database, and fills the cache.
CDNServers near users that cache content.
Circuit breakerStops calls to a failing dependency for a while.
Consistent hashingMaps keys and servers on a ring so few keys move when servers change.
CQRSSeparate models for writes and reads.
Error budgetThe failure allowed by an SLO over a period.
Fencing tokenAn increasing number that rejects writes from stale holders.
IdempotencyDoing an operation twice has the same effect as once.
Idempotency keyClient-chosen ID that lets the server recognise a repeat.
OutboxEvent saved in the same transaction as the change, then published.
PartitionA slice of data or a log, handled by one node.
QuorumEnough replicas answering to guarantee overlap.
RPO / RTOHow much data you may lose / how long recovery may take.
SagaA sequence of steps, each with a compensation to undo it.
SLOA target for a service level, such as 99.9% of requests under 300 ms.
WatermarkThe point in event time before which no late events are expected.
